1001.event_title: Hetty Green, America's richest woman, lives in cheap lodgings
1001.place: New York City and Hoboken, New Jersey, United States
1001.event: Hetty Green inherited about 10 million dollars in 1865 and, through shrewd investment and lending on Wall Street, became reputedly the wealthiest woman in the United States, leaving an estate of more than 100 million dollars when she died in 1916. Despite her fortune she lived with her children in inexpensive rented lodgings, for years in a small apartment in Hoboken, avoiding any display of wealth and virtually all society. Newspapers circulated many stories of her frugality, some of them exaggerated, and she became known as the Witch of Wall Street.
1001.explanation: Green's vast fortune grew year after year while she herself lived as though she had very little of it.
1001.tie_back: The kural says that a man who fills his house with vast wealth and never enjoys it is as good as dead, since his wealth does nothing through him, and Green amassed immense riches that she scarcely allowed herself to use.
1001._accuracy_note: A strong fit for wealth amassed but not enjoyed; some sources note that she gave discreetly and that the press exaggerated her miserliness.

1002.event_title: Didius Julianus buys the support of the Praetorian Guard
1002.event: After the Praetorian Guard killed the emperor Pertinax in March 193, the wealthy senator Didius Julianus competed with Pertinax's father-in-law, Sulpicianus, for the Guard's backing by promising each soldier a cash payment, and won with the larger offer. The Guard proclaimed him emperor, but his rule was insecure from the start, and when the general Septimius Severus marched on Rome with the Danube legions, support for Julianus collapsed. He was put to death on 1 June 193, about two months after his accession.
1002.explanation: Julianus's wealth bought him the title of emperor but none of the loyalty or legitimacy needed to keep it.
1002.tie_back: The kural describes the delusion of thinking that wealth can do everything, and Julianus's brief, doomed reign shows how badly that belief can end.
1002._accuracy_note: A good fit for the delusion that money achieves all; the kural's picture of a miser who clings to his wealth and gives nothing away does not match a man who spent heavily, and the event appears elsewhere in the book.

1003.event_title: Verres plunders Sicily and is driven into exile
1003.place: Sicily and Rome, Roman Republic (now Italy)
1003.event: Gaius Verres governed the Roman province of Sicily from 73 to 71 BCE and used his office to extort money and seize works of art and other valuables from its people. In 70 BCE the Sicilians engaged Marcus Tullius Cicero to prosecute him for extortion; Cicero gathered evidence across the island in a few weeks and opened the case so forcefully that Verres's advocate, Hortensius, gave up the defence. Verres left Rome for exile before the trial ended, and Cicero's published speeches made his name a byword for official greed.
1003.explanation: Verres pursued gain with no concern for his reputation, and what survives of him is a lasting record of disgrace.
1003.tie_back: The kural says that men greedy only for piling up wealth, with no care for an honourable name, are a burden to the earth, and Verres enriched himself at the expense of an entire province.
1003._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for greed indifferent to honour, though our knowledge comes largely from his prosecutor's speeches; the event also appears elsewhere in the book.

1004.event_title: The miser John Camden Neild leaves his fortune to Queen Victoria
1004.place: Chelsea, London, and North Marston, Buckinghamshire, United Kingdom
1004.event: John Camden Neild inherited a fortune of about 250,000 pounds from his father in 1814 and lived as a recluse and miser in his house in Cheyne Walk, Chelsea. When he died in August 1852 his will left almost his entire estate, then worth about 500,000 pounds, to Queen Victoria, whom he had never met, while making no provision for his longtime servants. The Queen increased the small bequests to his executors, provided for his servants, and later restored the chancel of North Marston church, where he was buried, inserting a window in his memory.
1004.explanation: Neild left behind no circle of family or friends, and the only lasting memorial to him was raised by a stranger who had received his money.
1004.tie_back: The kural asks what a man whom no one loves can expect to leave behind, and Neild's long, solitary hoarding left nothing of him but a bequest to someone he had never known.
1004._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for an unloved man's empty legacy, though the sources describe his isolation and miserliness rather than directly documenting that no one cared for him.

1005.event_title: Russell Sage dies with 70 million dollars after a lifetime of tight-fistedness
1005.event: Russell Sage, a financier who helped organise American railroads and telegraphs and became a major Wall Street moneylender, died in 1906 with a fortune estimated at about 70 million dollars. He was known for his frugality, and over a marriage of 37 years he and his wife made only three major charitable gifts. His widow, Margaret Olivia Sage, then gave the fortune away, beginning with 10 million dollars in 1907 to establish the Russell Sage Foundation for the improvement of social and living conditions in the United States.
1005.explanation: Sage's fortune did almost nothing for anyone in his own lifetime; it became a force for good only once it passed out of his hands.
1005.tie_back: The kural says that for those who neither give nor enjoy, wealth counts for nothing even if they own crores heaped upon crores, and Sage's millions achieved nothing until his widow gave them away.
1005._accuracy_note: A good fit for wealth neither given nor enjoyed; the claim about his stinginess rests on his reputation and the record of the couple's few gifts rather than on a single documented act.

1006.event_title: J. Paul Getty installs a pay telephone at Sutton Place
1006.place: Sutton Place, Surrey, England, United Kingdom
1006.event: After the American oil billionaire J. Paul Getty, then counted among the richest men in the world, made the Tudor mansion Sutton Place in Surrey his base in 1959, Time reported that he had cut back the gardening staff and installed a pay telephone for visitors' use. Getty later explained in his autobiography that the coin-box phone was a response to soaring telephone bills run up by the many people passing through the house during renovations. The public nonetheless took the pay phone as a symbol of his tightness with money, and it became the best-known story of his frugality.
1006.explanation: The story stuck to Getty because it seemed to sum up a vast fortune that its owner was reluctant to share even in small ways.
1006.tie_back: The kural calls a man who neither enjoys his wealth nor is disposed to give to others a blight upon that wealth, and the pay telephone became the public emblem of a fortune held back even from guests.
1006._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Getty did enjoy his wealth (notably in collecting art) and founded a major museum, and he gave a practical reason for the pay phone, so the episode fits the public image more than the facts of his character.

1007.event_title: Bokassa crowns himself emperor amid national poverty
1007.place: Bangui, Central African Empire (now Central African Republic)
1007.event: On 4 December 1977 Jean-Bedel Bokassa, ruler of the Central African Republic, which he had renamed the Central African Empire, crowned himself Emperor Bokassa I in a ceremony modelled on Napoleon's coronation, seated on a great gilded eagle throne. Britannica puts the cost at more than 20 million dollars, an enormous sum for one of the poorest countries in the world, and much of it was met by France. The spectacle drew international criticism, and Bokassa was overthrown in 1979.
1007.explanation: Bokassa spent a fortune on his own glory in a country where most people lacked basic services, and the money vanished in a single ceremony.
1007.tie_back: The kural says that the wealth of one who gives nothing to the destitute is wasted like great beauty growing old alone, and Bokassa poured national wealth into one day's display while his people remained poor.
1007._accuracy_note: A reasonable but partial fit: the coronation shows wealth withheld from the destitute and wasted, but it was largely public and foreign money rather than a private hoard.

1008.event_title: Ceausescu clears a Bucharest district for the House of the People
1008.event: From 1984 the Romanian leader Nicolae Ceausescu had an enormous palace built in the centre of Bucharest as a new political and administrative centre, on the site of the old Uranus district, a hillside neighbourhood of small cobbled streets and older houses that was demolished for the project. The construction required clearing large areas of the historic downtown. The building was still unfinished inside when Ceausescu fell in December 1989, and since 1991 it has housed Romania's Parliament.
1008.explanation: The colossal palace stood in the heart of the capital as a monument to the ruler rather than a benefit to the people whose homes it replaced.
1008.tie_back: The kural likens the wealth of a man whom nobody loves to a poisonous tree bearing fruit in the middle of the town, and Ceausescu's vast palace rose in the centre of Bucharest offering nothing to the citizens around it.
1008._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for the image of unwanted wealth in the town centre, though the palace was built with state resources rather than one man's private fortune, and the project appears elsewhere in the book.

1009.event_title: Louis XIV seizes Fouquet's wealth and takes his artists for Versailles
1009.event: Nicolas Fouquet, Louis XIV's superintendent of finances, amassed a vast fortune and built the magnificent chateau of Vaux-le-Vicomte, where he entertained the king at a lavish fete on 17 August 1661. Less than three weeks later, on 5 September 1661, he was arrested at Nantes and charged over his handling of state finances; his assets were seized, and many works of art from Vaux passed into the royal collections. The king took into his own service Fouquet's architect Louis Le Vau, painter Charles Le Brun and garden designer Andre Le Notre, with the team of craftsmen they had assembled, and set them to work on Versailles, while Fouquet spent the rest of his life in prison.
1009.explanation: The splendour Fouquet had built up passed almost overnight to the king, who used it to create something even grander for himself.
1009.tie_back: The kural says that shining wealth gathered without regard for virtue will in the end be taken by others, and Fouquet's fortune, artists and treasures were taken over by the king.
1009._accuracy_note: A strong fit for wealth taken by others; historians still debate how far Fouquet was actually guilty, and the kural's elements of forsaking love and self-denial are not clearly present. The event also appears elsewhere in the book.

1010.event_title: Mark Twain recovers from bankruptcy and repays his creditors
1010.place: United States and a world lecture tour
1010.event: In 1894 Mark Twain's publishing firm, Charles L. Webster and Company, failed and, weakened further by heavy losses on the Paige typesetting machine, he was forced into personal bankruptcy. Though not legally required to repay his creditors in full, he resolved to do so, set out on a lecture tour around the world in 1895-96 and published an account of it, Following the Equator, in 1897. By 1898 the earnings from the tour and the book, with the help of his friend Henry H. Rogers's management of his money, had allowed him to pay his creditors in full.
1010.explanation: Twain's reputation and talent remained intact through his financial collapse, and within a few years they had restored his fortune.
1010.tie_back: The kural says that the brief poverty of an honoured rich man is like a rain cloud that has emptied itself for a while and will soon be full again, and Twain's honoured name refilled his empty purse within four years.
1010._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for a temporary poverty quickly refilled, but Twain's ruin came from bad investments rather than from generosity, and the event also appears elsewhere in the book.
